Moving horizon estimation for linear models

Source: R/mhe.R
ctrl_mhe.Rd

Estimate the state of \(x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k + G w_k\), \(y_k = C x_k + D u_k + v_k\) by solving, at each sample \(T\), the finite-horizon problem over the window \(s = T - N + 1, \ldots, T\): $$\min_{x_s, \ldots, x_T,\, w_s, \ldots, w_{T-1}} \|x_s - \bar x_s\|^2_{P_s^{-1}} + \sum_{j=s}^{T-1} \|w_j\|^2_{Q_n^{-1}} + \sum_{j=s}^{T} \|y_j - C x_j - D u_j\|^2_{R_n^{-1}}$$ subject to the model equations and optional bounds on the states and the process noise. The estimate is \(\hat x_{T|T} = x_T\).

Usage

ctrl_mhe(
  sys,
  horizon,
  Qn,
  Rn,
  G = NULL,
  x0 = NULL,
  P0 = NULL,
  x_min = -Inf,
  x_max = Inf,
  w_min = -Inf,
  w_max = Inf,
  solver_settings = list()
)

ctrl_mhe_run(mhe, y, u = NULL, warm_start = TRUE)

Arguments

sys

Discrete time ctrl_ss model.

horizon

Window length N (number of measurements in the window).

Qn, Rn

Process and measurement noise covariances (positive definite).

G

Process noise input matrix (default identity).

x0, P0

Prior mean and covariance at the first sample.

x_min, x_max

Bounds on the states.

w_min, w_max

Bounds on the process noise.

solver_settings

OSQP settings.

mhe

A ctrl_mhe object.

y

Measurements (T x p, NA rows are missing samples).

u

Inputs (T x m) or NULL.

warm_start

Start each window's QP from the previous window's solution, shifted by one sample (the new last state is the model prediction and the new last disturbance is zero). This changes only the number of OSQP iterations, not the solution.

Value

An object of class ctrl_mhe; run it with ctrl_mhe_run().

A list of class ctrl_mhe_result with estimates (T x n, row k is \(\hat x_{k|k}\)), status (OSQP status per sample), objective, iterations and solve_time.

Details

Arrival cost. The first term summarizes the data before the window. The prior mean is the prediction from the previous MHE estimate, \(\bar x_s = A \hat x_{s-1|s-1} + B u_{s-1}\), and \(P_s\) follows the Kalman filter covariance recursion. Without active constraints this makes MHE coincide with the Kalman filter (which the tests verify); with active constraints MHE differs from, and can improve on, the Kalman filter, at the price of one QP per sample, so its cost grows with the horizon. MHE is worth it when states or noises have hard physical bounds (concentrations, saturations) that the Kalman filter would violate.

Each window QP is assembled from scratch and solved by OSQP.

Examples

sys <- ctrl_ss(0.9, 1, 1, dt = 1)
mhe <- ctrl_mhe(sys, horizon = 5, Qn = 0.01, Rn = 0.1, x_min = 0)
est <- ctrl_mhe_run(mhe, y = c(0.2, -0.1, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1, 0.5))
est$estimates
#>              x1
#> [1,] 0.18181818
#> [2,] 0.04356436
#> [3,] 0.15438123
#> [4,] 0.18145126
#> [5,] 0.14818606
#> [6,] 0.21654918
